entry.title: ABAP Debugger Enhancement — Reloaded: Typed VALUE Statements and What's Changed Since 2019
entry.content:
This post was first published on LinkedIn. A German version is available on the T5 website.

The debugger often shows you exactly the data you need for a unit test — and then you end up retyping it by hand. DDVE (Debugger Data View Extension) saves you that step: one click, and you get a ready-to-paste VALUE statement. The latest update makes that statement typed and closes a few long-standing gaps — and since the last blog post in 2019, the community has contributed quite a bit as well.

How it works

DDVE adds a “Data for ABAP View” entry to the debugger in three places: the Services of the Tool menus of the table and structure tools, and the toolbar of the table's ALV display. The result is a syntactically correct, pretty-printed statement like this, ready to be copied into your test method:

" One click in the debugger turns the content of LT_FLIGHTS into:
DATA(lt_flights) = VALUE tt_flights(
  ( carrid = 'LH' connid = '0400' fldate = '20260115' price = '666.00' currency = 'EUR' )
  ( carrid = 'LH' connid = '0402' fldate = '20260116' price = '471.00' currency = 'EUR' )
  ( carrid = 'AA' connid = '0017' fldate = '20260117' price = '422.94' currency = 'USD' ) ).

 

The custom entry “Data for ABAP View” in the service menu of the table or structure view

The result popup with the generated, ready-to-paste VALUE statement

Under the hood, DDVE plugs into the standard debugger through three implicit enhancements — no modifications. All three hand over to the same pipeline: read the real data, resolve the type, render the VALUE statement, then format and show it.

Architecture overview: three implicit enhancements in the standard ABAP debugger hand over to the DDVE pipeline

 

New name, new home

If you know the tool from my earlier posts here on SAP Community from 2017 and 2019: it has since been refactored, extended and renamed, and it now lives in a new GitHub repository:

https://github.com/gepparta/abap_debugger_data_view_extension

I was also happy to find DDVE in the DSAG ABAP guide: the ABAP guidelines of the German-speaking SAP user group list it as the SAP GUI option for generating VALUE statements from debugger data.

All classes follow the ZCL_DDVE_* naming scheme. New in this update:

  1. Typed VALUE statements with inline declarations — DATA(flights) = VALUE flighttab( ... ) instead of an untyped #
  2. Robustness fixes for nested data in filtered exports, anonymous runtime types and empty tables and structures
  3. A refactored core with a much broader unit test suite

And since 2019, the community has contributed an ALV export that respects filters, hidden columns and sort order, .INCLUDE support and fixes for hashed tables — more on that below.

 

New in this update

1. Typed VALUE statements with inline declaration

Until now the generated statement looked like lt_flights = VALUE #( ... ) — fine as long as the target variable already exists and the compiler can infer the type. In a fresh unit test it usually can't.

Typed statements were an old feature request by Timo John — now they're here. DDVE resolves the variable's type from the debugger context and generates a self-contained inline declaration:

" DDIC type
DATA(table_of_flights) = VALUE flighttab( ( carrid = 'AA' connid = '0017' ) ).

" type declared inside a global class
DATA(item) = VALUE zcl_order=>ty_item( col1 = 1 ).

The interesting part is what counts as a usable type name. The debugger reports absolute type names such as \CLASS=ZCL_ORDER\TYPE=TY_ITEM or \PROGRAM=ZREP\TYPE=TY_LOCAL. Where no usable type or variable name can be derived — e.g. for a component path like LS_X-COMP — DDVE gracefully falls back to the classic untyped VALUE #( ... ), since DATA(...) with # would not compile. A new class ZCL_DDVE_TYPE_RESOLVER translates the debugger's type names into source-code-valid expressions:

Debugger type name Generated expression Why it works in a test

\TYPE=SFLIGHTsflightDDIC, visible everywhere
\CLASS=ZCL_X\TYPE=TY_Yzcl_x=>ty_ypublic always, private via LOCAL FRIENDS
\INTERFACE=ZIF_X\TYPE=TY_Yzif_x=>ty_yinterface components are public
\PROGRAM=ZREP\TYPE=TY_LOCALty_localtest include sits in the same program
\TYPE-POOL=ABAP\TYPE=ABAP_BOOLabap_booltype pools are global
procedure-local / generated typesfallback #not addressable from a test

2. Robustness fixes for the tricky cases

A couple of long-standing edge cases are gone:

  • Nested data in filtered exports — since the filter support from 2023 (see the community section below), nested tables and structures in the ALV export came out as placeholder texts like COL2 = `Structure: flat, not charlike` . When the debugger's ALV works on an internal copy of the table, DDVE now re-reads the real data and uses the ALV view only as a row and column mask — filters, hidden columns and sort order still apply, and nested data keeps its real values.
  • Anonymous runtime types — inline declared table types, OCCURS header lines, TYPE HANDLE structures — are now reconstructed from debugger metadata instead of silently producing no output popup at all.
  • Empty tables and structures produce a valid empty VALUE statement instead of broken output.

3. A refactored core with a broader test suite

The 2019 post already talked about single responsibility; this iteration went further. Rendering of VALUE expressions now lives in a dedicated class (ZCL_DDVE_VALUE_RENDERER) that owns the entire recursion for nested data, while the debugger facades for tables and structures only orchestrate. Output (CL_DEMO_OUTPUT), customizing access and pretty-printer creation are isolated behind their own small classes — which is precisely why the package now comes with a much broader ABAP Unit test suite, most of it mock-free.

Since 2019: contributions from the community

Between 2020 and 2023, several pull requests made it into the tool without ever getting a blog post of their own. If you still run the 2019 version, they are new for you as well.

What you see is what you get

Thanks to Daniel Wegner (@WegnerDan), the export respects what you see in the debugger's ALV:

  • Rows filtered out in the ALV are excluded from the generated statement.
  • Columns hidden in the ALV layout (no_out) are skipped.
  • The export follows the current ALV sort order.
  • The ALV's technical INDEX column no longer ends up in the generated statement.

So you can shape your test data visually in the ALV before exporting it — a surprisingly effective way to cut a 500-row production table down to the three rows that actually reproduce your bug.

More contributions

  • .INCLUDE structures — @juancarlosrodriguezf made sure that structures containing .INCLUDEs (e.g. a local type that includes T000 plus extra fields) are flattened correctly into the field catalog. Previously the included components were lost; the fix ships with its own unit test.
  • Hashed tables and performance — @sandraros contributed faster statement generation plus fixes for hashed tables and for tables with a component named INDEX.
  • Pretty printer and housekeeping — Andreas Kopp (@andkopp) fixed details in the pretty printer, and Christian Günter (@christianguenter2) brought the repository in line with the current abapGit format and fixed a syntax error.

Thanks to everyone who contributed! Two related posts here on SAP Community: Fork of ABAP Debugger Data View Extension tool and Speed up regression tests with the ABAP debugger, which uses the tool to create test data for regression tests.

A note on the built-in pretty printer

The 2019 post made quite a fuss about pretty printing the generated VALUE statement — including the option to plug in your own printer implementation via a pretty printer interface (today ZIF_DDVE_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER) and the customizing table ZTOP_DVE_CUST.

Honestly, this part has become less important: with ABAP Cleaner there is now an excellent open source formatter that aligns VALUE constructor expressions beautifully in ADT. So a perfectly fine workflow today is: export the raw statement with DDVE, paste it into your test method, and let ABAP Cleaner take care of the formatting.

The built-in pretty printers (and the customizing mechanism) are still there and still useful if you want a readable preview right in the SAP GUI popup — but if you are an ADT + ABAP Cleaner user, don't worry too much about this feature.

Migrating from the old installation

If you still run the original version (ZCL_OP_* classes), note that the enhancement implementations and the customizing table have the same names in both versions. Therefore:

  1. Export your ZTOP_DVE_CUST entries (if any).
  2. Uninstall the old package via abapGit (Uninstall/Purge).
  3. Pull the DDVE repository.
  4. Re-import your customizing and map the class names: ZCL_OP_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER → ZCL_DDVE_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER, ZCL_MAX_LINE_LENGTH_PP → ZCL_DDVE_MAX_LINE_LENGTH_PP.

Do not install both versions in parallel.

Prerequisites

NetWeaver ABAP 7.40 SP08 or higher.

How to install

All the coding is available here:

https://github.com/gepparta/abap_debugger_data_view_extension

Please use abapGit to get the coding into your system.

Pull requests and issues on GitHub are welcome.

Hands up: who has already used the extension? Or have you all moved on to ADT or VS Code and left the SAP GUI debugger behind – or is AI writing your unit tests by now anyway? Let me know in the comments.

entry.title: What's New in SAP Automation Pilot – Q3 2026
entry.content:
SAP Automation Pilot ships 15 new features in Q3 2026 – including native AI-agent authentication, a persistent key-value storage shared across executions, and over 60 new provided commands.

If you're running automations on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), your toolkit just got a serious upgrade. This quarter touches everything from how you connect to external systems, to how automations persist data between runs, to how you track what's actually happening across your landscape. Here's the full picture.

 

New to the product?​

It's a low-code/no-code automation service on SAP BTP that helps DevOps and Operations teams automate cloud operations – with over 300 built-in commands and a serverless script execution environment. More details about the product can be found at:

  • SAP Automation Pilot Documentation

Usage Statistics Dashboard

SAP Automation Pilot now has a built-in dashboard that shows you how your automations are actually being used. You can see the number of executions by day and hour, which commands get triggered most, success rates, and how much of your quota you've consumed – all with time-range filtering. If you've been piecing this picture together manually or through external tools, it's now right inside the service. For more information, see Working with Executions.

Subexecutions Panel in Execution Details

When you open an execution's details page, there's now a dedicated Subexecutions section that lists everything the parent execution triggered. Subexecutions also get tagged automatically – autopi:parentExecutorPath tells you which executor started them, and for ParallelForEach, autopi:parentBatchIndex tells you which batch they belonged to. No more jumping back and forth to understand what a complex command actually did. For more information, see Monitoring Executions.

Capture HTTP User-Agent as a Service Tag

When an external system triggers an execution via the API, SAP Automation Pilot now reads the User-Agent header from the HTTP request and stores it as a read-only autopi:userAgent service tag. This means that even when multiple systems share the same service account, you can tell which one triggered which execution – directly from the details page or by filtering via the API. It takes zero configuration on the SAP Automation Pilot side – the caller just needs to set a meaningful User-Agent header, which is a one-line change in any HTTP request. For more information, see Tags.

Configurable Table Columns with Custom Tag-Based Columns

The entity tables in SAP Automation Pilot – Commands, Inputs, Executions, Scheduled Executions – can now be personalized. You can show or hide predefined columns, reorder them, and add custom columns based on your tag keys. So if your team tags executions by environment, region, or ticket number, those values can now show up as their own columns instead of being buried inside each execution's detail view. For more information, see Configuring Table Columns.

Command Clone with Multiple Cloning Modes

Cloning commands now gives you three distinct modes. Clone Full Command copies the entire configuration into a new command, so you can adapt and extend it without touching the source – this one is available for custom commands. Clone Contract Only keeps the same input and output keys but gives you an empty implementation to build from scratch. Clone as Wrapper creates a new command with a single executor that calls the source command, with all parameters automatically mapped – so you can add logic around it without reconfiguring anything manually. Both Clone Contract Only and Clone as Wrapper are available for provided commands as well, giving you a proper starting point when building on top of SAP-provided content. For more information, see Cloning Commands.

Secure Service Account Integration for AI Agents

Service accounts in SAP Automation Pilot now support token-based authentication – meaning the credentials can be used as a Bearer token or an API key, on top of the existing Basic authentication. The service account type has been renamed to API Token / Basic and the password field is now called token to reflect this.

 

 

Why does this matter? Because MCP clients, Joule, and most third-party agent frameworks expect token-based auth. Until now, wiring them into SAP Automation Pilot required workarounds. Now it's a native, one-step setup. Alongside this, a new MCP permission lets you scope exactly which MCP server endpoints a service account can access – so you can give an AI agent the ability to trigger automations without granting access to anything beyond what the agent needs.

If you're building agent-driven Ops workflows, this is the feature that makes it practical. For more information, see Managing Service Account Permissions.

Native Destination Service Integration & HTTP Request Enhancements

The new HttpRequestViaDestination command lets you execute HTTP requests by referencing a destination from the SAP Destination Service directly. URL resolution, authentication, proxy settings, certificates – all of it is pulled from the destination configuration automatically. No more duplicating credentials and connection details inside SAP Automation Pilot. If you're already managing your connectivity through the SAP Destination Service, your automations can now plug straight into that setup. For more information see HTTP Operations (http-sapcp) Catalog.

SendEmail STARTTLS Support

The SendEmail command now supports STARTTLS encryption through a new encryptionMode input key. Previously, sending emails through public SMTP servers that require STARTTLS meant routing traffic through SAP Cloud Connector. Now you can connect directly – one less hop, one less thing to configure. For more information, see Email Operations (email-sapcp) Catalog.

Cross-Execution Runtime Storage

Until now, each execution in SAP Automation Pilot lived in isolation – once it finished, its data went with it. That changes with the new Cross-Execution Runtime Storage: a tenant-scoped, encrypted key/value storage that any execution can read from and write to. Three commands handle everything – PutValue, GetValue, and DeleteValue.

This unlocks automation scenarios that simply weren't practical before. Executions can now pass state to each other, track progress across multi-step workflows, cache shared configuration, or coordinate processes – all without relying on external storage. If you've ever built a workaround to share data between executions, this is the clean, built-in replacement. For more information, see Execution Runtime Storage.

SAP Integration Suite Provided Catalog

SAP Automation Pilot now ships a dedicated catalog for SAP Integration Suite – 21 ready-to-use commands covering integration flow lifecycle management, configuration updates, monitoring of deployed integration flows, and directory management. All accessible directly from the provided catalogs, no custom command building required.

This is a significant expansion. SAP Integration Suite is one of the most widely used services on SAP BTP, and until now, automating operations around it meant building everything from scratch using HTTP requests. With a provided catalog in place, teams can automate routine integration operations – deploying flows, checking statuses, updating configurations.

If you're managing integration landscapes at scale, this catalog saves a lot of custom work. For more information, see SAP Integration Suite (is-sapcp) Catalog.

SAP HANA Cloud Lifecycle Management Commands

A new SAP HANA Cloud Administration catalog brings 40 commands for managing SAP HANA Cloud instances – covering provisioning, lifecycle management, configuration, and observability across both Cloud Foundry and Other Environment deployment types.
We covered this catalog in depth in a dedicated blog post – you can find it here: Meet the SAP HANA Cloud Administration Catalog for SAP Automation Pilot

Granular Skip Options for ParallelForEach Failures

When a ParallelForEach step fails, the Skip dialog now offers two distinct options – skip only the current failed batch and continue processing the remaining ones, or skip all remaining batches and move on to the next executor in the parent command. Previously, skipping meant stopping everything. Now you can isolate a failure without halting the entire parallel run. For more information, see Controlling Executions with Actions.

Custom Tags for ParallelForEach Subexecutions

You can now assign tags to ParallelForEach subexecutions dynamically using expressions. Instead of entering tags manually for each subexecution, you reference a complete tag set from an input and it gets applied automatically, making it easier to organize, filter, and trace parallel workloads at scale. For more information, see ParallelForEach.

Auto-Abort Stale Failed Executions

A new Auto-Abort Failed Executions feature automatically aborts executions that remain in a Failed state without updates for a configurable duration (1–168 hours). Your execution list stays clean without manual intervention. For more information, see Additional Features.

Immediate Deletion of Completed Executions

You can now delete completed executions on the spot instead of waiting for the retention cleanup cycle. Setting the retention value to 0 causes immediate deletion as soon as an execution reaches a completed status. When an execution is done and you no longer need it, it's gone, keeping your execution list manageable without relying on automated retention policies. For more information, see Additional Features.

Learn More & Stay Connected

  • What’s New in SAP Automation Pilot - full release notes and changelog

  • SAP Road Map Explorer for SAP Automation Pilot

  • Release Navigator for SAP Automation Pilot - find release notes, blog posts, and related resources in one place

  • Public GitHub SAP Automation Pilot sample use cases

  • SAP Automation Pilot Documentation

The Generate Compliance Forms option is displayed based on the following conditions:

  1. The candidate’s job country, job location, or home address country is either Canada or the United States.

entry.title: New Pattern: Migrating Content-Based Routing Synchronous Scenarios to SAP IS using Migration Tool
entry.content:
This blog post is part of the series Master Blog: SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration – Tool and Guidance . In this edition, we focus specifically on migrating Content-Based Routing (CBR) Synchronous Scenarios to SAP Integration Suite using the Migration Tool.  

What This Blog Covers

The Migration Tool in SAP Integration Suite now supports CBR Synchronous scenarios. This post walks you through everything you need to migrate one: 

  • What makes a CBR scenario synchronous  and the one constraint that sets it apart from async CBR 
  • The eight supported CBR Standard Synchronous cases, broken down by operations, receivers, and interfaces 
  • How the Migration Tool detects the pattern from your ICO automatically 
  • What the Standard Approach generates, and where it differs from the async migration 
  • How the Pipeline Approach works : the three flows, the Partner Directory, and the receiverDetermination XSLT 
  • What to check before you go live

Understanding Synchronous Content-Based Routing in SAP PO 

In a Content-Based Routing scenario, a message does not arrive with a fixed destination. The runtime inspects the message payload, evaluates it against the conditions defined in Receiver Determination, and selects the receiver at that moment. The routing is governed entirely by the content of the message: a field value, an element, or a structure within the payload. 

In practice, this means the following: 

  • Several receivers are configured, and each is associated with its own routing condition. 
  • The decision is dynamic. The same configuration can deliver different messages to different systems according to their content. 
  • A receiver may require the message in a specific format. Through Interface Determination, the same incoming message can be mapped differently depending on which receiver is selected. 

If you are new to Content-Based Routing (CBR) in SAP PO, we recommend first reading our earlier blog Migrating Content-Based Routing Scenarios Using th... - SAP Community  which explains how CBR works, including Receiver Determination and Interface Determination in detail. 

On top of everything CBR already does, the synchronous variant adds one thing: the sender waits for a response.

What Makes it Synchronous? 

Three things together define this as a synchronous scenario: 

  • Both sides use synchronous interfaces

             In SAP PO, a synchronous service interface defines both a request message and a corresponding response message. It's a two-way contract from the start something goes in, something comes back. An asynchronous interface only defines one direction. 

  • Two-Directional Message Mappings

             Because the sender and receiver typically have different formats, two mappings are required:

  •     Request Mapping : transforms the sender's payload into the format the receiver expects 
  •     Response Mapping : transforms the receiver's reply into the format the sender expects 
  • The Connection Stays Open 

             The sender sends the message and waits. It doesn't move on until a reply comes back on the same connection. If something  goes wrong such as a routing issue, a mapping failure, a timeout the sender still needs an answer. Even if it's an error, the caller is waiting. 

            One rule that changes everything 

             In asynchronous CBR, you can route to multiple receivers at once, each gets their own copy. Synchronous doesn't work that way. The sender is waiting for one response, so the routing must land on exactly one receiver and one interface. This means your routing conditions need to be set up so only one can ever match at a time. If two conditions match the same message, things break. If none match, the scenario must throw an error because the sender hasn't moved on yet and is still waiting for a reply. 

Migration of CBR synchronous scenarios using Standard approach and Pipeline approach 

Supported Scenarios in CBR Standard Synchronous 

Every one of these uses a Local Rule with XPath for the routing conditions. 

One thing to keep in mind: when you have N receivers, each one needs its own routing condition, otherwise the scenario isn't valid.

Standard Synchronous Scenario in SAP PO 

 The scenario covered in this blog involves an ICO (Integration Configuration Object) with: 

  • Multiple receivers, each with its own receiver interface 
  • Routing conditions defined per receiver 
  • Standard Receiver Determination Type (operation-specific) 
  • Both Receiver Determination and Interface Determination configured 

This represents one of the more complex real-world setups in SAP PO and the Migration Tool handles it end to end. 

Receiver Determination 

 

Interface Determination 

Picking the Right Pattern in the Migration Wizard 

In Step 3 where you have to Choose Pattern and Approach, the Migration Tool automatically detects the pattern based on your ICO configuration and presents Content-Based Routing Synchronous as the predefined migration pattern.  

At this step, you also select your approach: Standard or Pipeline. 

Standard Approach 

The Standard Approach for CBR synchronous migration follows the same structural pattern as the asynchronous CBR migration. For a full walkthrough of the inbound routing logic, Receiver Determination, Interface Determination, and outbound delivery refer to blog Migrating Content-Based Routing Scenarios Using th... - SAP Community. Below, we focus on what is specific to the synchronous pattern. 

Key Differences in the Synchronous Pattern 

  • Inbound Flow uses ProcessDirect Instead of JMS 

  This is the most fundamental infrastructure difference between the two patterns: 

 

Asynchronous CBR 

Synchronous CBR 

Adapter used 

JMS 

ProcessDirect 

Communication model 

Fire-and-forget . Message is queued 

Request-Reply 

Inbound flow behavior 

Hands off the message and exits 

Waits for a response before returning to sender 

In asynchronous CBR, the inbound flow hands the message to a JMS queue and its job is done. In the synchronous pattern, JMS cannot be used, it is a one-way, queue-based mechanism with no return path. Instead, the inbound flow uses a ProcessDirect adapter with a Request Reply step to call the next flow directly and stays connected until a response comes back. That response is then returned to the sender on the same channel. 

  • Routing must land on exactly one receiver 

The Groovy script evaluates conditions the same way it does in async CBR. The difference is what happens with the result in synchronous; it must resolve to exactly one receiver and one interface. You can't route to two receivers at once because there's only one connection open and one response expected. 

If two conditions match the same message, the behavior is unpredictable. If none match, the flow must throw an error because the sender is still waiting for a reply. 

  • The outbound flow also sends a response back 

In asynchronous CBR, the outbound flow delivers the request and is done. In the synchronous pattern, it has to do the return trip too: 

Direction 

What Happens 

Request 

Routes using the SAP_Receiver header, applies the request mapping, delivers to the receiver 

Response 

Gets the reply back, applies the response mapping, cleans up internal headers, and returns it to the sender 

Without the response mapping and the header cleanup, the response never makes it back cleanly. Both steps matter.

Pipeline Approach 

This section demonstrates the Pipeline Approach for migrating the same scenario. A pipeline represents the complete set of processing steps for a message. It consists of a set of pipeline elements that call pipeline services - for example, carrying out mappings or routing messages to different receivers. 

Before going further, we recommend reading Introducing the new pipeline concept in Cloud Inte... - SAP Community which takes us through the basics of pipeline concept.

For a deeper understanding of the Pipeline Approach, please refer to the following references: 

Migration Tooling now supporting migration via the pipeline approach 

Applying the pipeline concept for an integration scenario in general 

Learn here the differences and characteristics of each approach to choose the one that aligns best with your migration needs Standard vs Pipeline Approach

 

Key Highlights in the Migration Wizard for Pipeline Approach 

Once the Pipeline Approach is selected in Step 3, the Migration Tool enables you to: 

  • Review and adjust alternative partner details if needed before anything is finalized 
  • Verify or update receiver and interface conditions that were migrated from SAP PO, if needed 

This review step is your safety net, catch anything that needs adjusting before the artifacts are generated. 

What Gets Generated After a Successful Migration 

Once the migration completes, the tool presents a full overview of all generated artifacts.  

On the first tab, you can see all three integration flows that were created, one scenario-specific inbound flow and two scenario-specific outbound flows (one per receiver-interface combination). Clicking the View Artifact button navigates you directly to each flow in Cloud Integration.

The PID and Its Parameters 

A Partner ID (PID) is created along with all associated configuration parameters. The Partner Directory tab gives you a structured view of everything that was generated and how it's connected together. 

For a deeper dive into how the Partner Directory works within the Pipeline concept, refer to: Using the Partner Directory in the Pipeline Concept 

 

The receiverDetermination Binary Parameter — Where Your Routing Lives 

Inside the Binary Parameters tab, a parameter named receiverDetermination is automatically created with an XSL content type. 

This is the one that does all the routing work at runtime. It contains the XSLT logic that reads your incoming message and decides which receiver gets it. Think of it as your CBR routing conditions — just packaged as an XSLT and stored in the Partner Directory instead of sitting inside the flow.  

A look at the generated XSLT 

 

The XSLT evaluates XPath expressions against the incoming message content to determine the appropriate receiver and interface. Here is how the routing logic looks: 

Condition 1: 

<xsl:if test="(/p1:MT_JOAH_Employee_REQ/Employee/FirstName = 'Marina')"> 

If FirstName is Marina, then the message is routed to receiver BC_PIELE_Receiver_2 and interface /Demo_CBR_Sync_pip_Blog/pip07/BC_PIELE_Receiver_2/IFIndex1 is called. 

Condition 2: 

<xsl:if test="(/p1:MT_JOAH_Employee_REQ/Employee/FirstName = 'John')"> 

If FirstName is John, then the message is routed to receiver BC_PIELE_Receiver and interface /Demo_CBR_Sync_pip_Blog/pip07/BC_PIELE_Receiver/IFIndex1 is called. 

And if nothing matches? The message isn't quietly dropped. The XSLT raises an error, so nothing gets misrouted. 

Integration Flow in Cloud Integration 

Inbound Integration Process (Scenario-Specific) 

 

 

 

This is where the message enters the pipeline. The sender adapter receives it, and the flow sets three headers: SAP_Sender, SAP_SenderInterface, and SAP_MessageType  which drive everything that follows. If the message needs format conversion before it goes further (JSON to XML, for example), a local subprocess takes care of that first. 

From there, the flow calls the generic synchronous runtime using a ProcessDirect adapter with a Request Reply step  and waits. When the response comes back, it can convert the format again if needed (XML to JSON), cleans up the pipeline headers, and returns the response to the sender. If anything fails at any point, an Exception SubProcess steps in and sends a structured error back  so the caller always gets a reply, success or failure. 

Integrated Messaging Runtime Sync (Generic) 

 

This is the second flow : Pipeline v2 Generic Step02 - Integrated Messaging Runtime Sync, available in the Cloud Integration Pipeline – Generic Pipelines package under Discover → Integrations. 

The important thing about this flow: it's shared. You deploy it once and every sync scenario uses it. It's called directly by the inbound flow via ProcessDirect and handles the central runtime logic for synchronous message processing. 

To explore the full details of how synchronous scenarios work within the Pipeline concept, check out the official SAP documentation: Integrated Messaging Runtime (Synchronous) | SAP Help Portal 

Outbound Processing (Scenario-Specific) 

 

 

 

This is the third flow  and in our scenario there are two of them, one per receiver-interface combination. Each outbound flow handles one receiver: it maps the request into the receiver's format, delivers it via a Request Reply step, maps the response back, and passes it upstream. 

One outbound flow per receiver-interface combination, so if you have three receivers with two interfaces each, expect six outbound flows in total. 

 Post-Migration Checklist - What to Verify Before You Go Live 

A successful migration isn't a green light to deploy. Run your checks first. 

For Post-Migration activities, after successfully migrating CBR Integration flow, please refer to the section Post-Migration Activities – Key Points to Keep in Mind 

For other manual activities for specific scenarios, please refer to the section “Manual Activities Depending on Integration Scenario” the P2P Blog from series 

 Wrapping up 

Migrating a Content-Based Routing Synchronous scenario from SAP PO to SAP Integration Suite involves more than moving artifacts, it requires understanding the two-way communication model, ensuring the correct request and response mappings are in place, and verifying that routing logic is accurately preserved in the target environment. 

The Migration Tool simplifies this significantly by automatically detecting the pattern from your ICO, generating all necessary artifacts for both the Standard and Pipeline approaches, and providing a structured review step before anything is finalized. 

For the Pipeline Approach in particular, the receiverDetermination XSLT in the Partner Directory becomes the single source of truth for routing logic at runtime making it transparent, manageable, and easy to extend as your integration landscape grows. 

Whether you choose the Standard or Pipeline Approach depends on your landscape and operational requirements but with the Migration Tool, both paths are fully supported and ready for use.

entry.title: BTP Success Plans from SAP in Action with real Experiences from the Field
entry.content:
We recently ran a webinar on how the Advanced and Max Success Plans work for SAP Business AI Platform (BAIP) and SAP Business Technology (BTP) customers. Together with Amit Lodhe, Global Service Solution Advisory Leader for SAP Business AI Platform, and Dilek Cevikalp, Customer Success Manager for BTP and BAIP, we walked through what these service plans deliver, showed real customer engagements and discussed open questions.  

This post summarizes the key points for anyone who is currently evaluating Success Plans for BTP/ BAIP, thinking about AI adoption on BTP in general, or wondering how the new Success Plan approach compares to what they had before.

The challenges SAP BTP customers face today

Let me start with what we hear regularly from BTP customers. Three themes keep coming up:

  • Slow innovation speed and limited AI adoption. Customers have BTP in place, they see the potential of Business AI, but they struggle to move from "we should do something with AI" to an actual implementation path. And the technology landscape is evolving fast.
  • Increased risk from excessive customization. Many organizations carry a lot of custom logic. When they want to modernize or adopt new capabilities, the complexity of their landscape creates risk. They need expert guidance to make the right architectural decisions, not just documentation.
  • Lack of holistic integration across platforms and applications. BTP connects multiple SAP and non-SAP systems. Getting identity management, connectivity, security, and process orchestration right requires more than self-service content. It requires hands-on expertise at the right moment.

The Advanced and Max Success Plans are designed to address these (and other) challenges. They provide structured guidance, dedicated expertise, and a collaborative engagement model that goes well beyond reactive support.

What the Advanced and Max Success Plans cover for BTP and BAIP

The core idea is that you get a Customer Success Manager (CSM) who orchestrates a tailored Advanced Success plan for you. The CSM acts as your single point of coordination. They build your adoption plan, position the right services, order them, and orchestrate their delivery across quarters. For Max Success Plan this orchestrating role is called "Success Plan Manager", who also can support onsite.

On the expert side, so called Success Experts provide deep subject matter expertise to help you adopt, optimize, and get full value from your SAP cloud solutions. This is not a help desk. It is a structured engagement with regular service planning, adoption checkpoints, and innovation checkpoints throughout the year.

CSM and Success Expert collaboration model with regular checkpoints.

You might ask yourself how the different Success Plan tiers work in practice:

The Advanced Success Plan includes orchestration of the success plan with Success Expert sessions, innovation and adoption guidance, activation and optimization sessions, AI-driven quality and process guidance, and enhanced support SLAs (50% faster initial response on priority 2, 3, and 4 incidents). Compared to the former Preferred Success offering, the Advanced plan delivers more value at the same price point as the former Standard Preferred Success. Customers now get also activation and optimization sessions and Success Expert engagement included, which previously required the more expensive Expanded Edition.

The Max Success Plan adds everything from Advanced plus cross-solution process improvement services, transformation advisory services, tailored AI use case adoption services, the dedicated Success Plan Manager (an evolution of the TQM role), premium support response SLAs, and support case management assistance. 

The Max Success plan is designed for complex landscapes where customers need large-scale, on-site, workshop-type engagements that deliver highly customized results. These premium services are consumed against so called premium service days.

One key differentiator across both tiers is, that the services from the Advanced layer are unlimited. There is no cap on how many services can be delivered per year, as long as they are part of your service plan. To put that into perspective, Amit shared the example of a Japanese customer who consumed more than 120 services in 18 months.

Customer Example 1: From "Where do we start with AI?" to a concrete pilot

The first case study involves a utilities IT services provider. They are an internal shared services organization supporting multiple utilities businesses. They already had RISE with SAP and were actively using BTP. The foundation was in place so to say.

When their internal business units started requesting AI capabilities, the IT team was unsure and hit a wall. They had identified a compelling use case: automating business partner creation from incoming emails. But they had no AI expertise internally and no clear implementation path. Multiple AI use cases from different lines of business were piling up, with no way to evaluate or prioritize them.

Three Advanced Success Plan services were activated:

  • AI Readiness Workshop for SAP Business AI - a full-day session with the complete technical team of eight participants
  • AI Workshop - dedicated follow-up to deepen the practical understanding
  • Expert AI Guidance for BTP Implementation -after connecting the customer's team with an SAP AI expert

The structured engagement replaced uncertainty with clear steps. The AI Core architecture was explained, the pilot use case was defined, and the IT team came out of the workshops equipped to build AI use cases independently. The pilot scope was agreed, and the next phase involves expert engagement directly on the customer's own landscape, moving from learning to building.

This engagement is still in progress. Dilek the CSM continues to orchestrate follow-up services as the customer's AI journey evolves.

Customer Example 2: From architectural uncertainty to a go-live with 4,200 employees

The second case is a large grid operator with approximately 4,200 employees. Their goal was to roll out Work Zone Advanced as their central employee portal.

The challenges were different here but equally blocking. The architectural decision between Work Zone Standard and Work Zone Advanced was unresolved. Identity management was in conflict because Microsoft's and SAP's recommendations contradicted. And the manual effort in content provisioning put scalability at risk.

The Advanced Success Plan services here were the following:

  • Architecture Review for SAP Work Zone: expert validation of the right BTP approach
  • Expert Guidance: a full-day BTP workshop covering Work Zone architecture, Integration Suite, and AI services
  • Strategic Assessment: coordination to resolve the identity management conflict

All of this was orchestrated through Dilek the CSM. Multiple SAP specialists were brought in, each for their specific domain, but the customer had a single point of coordination throughout.

The result was the achieved go-live. All 4,200 employees are now live on Work Zone Advanced. The Standard vs. Advanced decision was made with confidence, without rework or guesswork. Identity management is resolved with clean authentication and security. The foundation is stable and scalable, with manual effort significantly reduced.

What is particularly interesting about this case is what happened next. The customer is now evaluating AI use cases including fraud detection and a payment verification agent. The CSM is already developing the next iteration of the success plan to cover these new priorities. That iterative nature of the engagement is central to how the model works.

The Success Plan service portfolio consists of more than 100 services

Behind the individual customer stories sits a comprehensive service portfolio. Amit walked us through what he called the "super catalogue". This are more than 100 services across all BTP modules.

The portfolio is structured around four promised outcomes:

  1. Continuous long-term engagement with increased productivity. The product expert helps you gain productivity in your execution, as both customer cases demonstrated.
  2. Reimagined processes and accelerated innovation. Through product guidance and innovation adoption guidance, manual and semi-automated processes are replaced.
  3. Adoption of next-generation capabilities and optimized processes with reduced TCO. Activation and optimization sessions involve hands-on configuration work done by SAP directly in your landscape. Trust management, IPS, IAS configuration, connectivity activation, Joule agent activation, AI Core activation — these are configurations that keep the ground ready. A recommendation is to separate core implementation activities (which you can leave for your partner) from non-core activation activities (divert those to the success plan).
  4. Improved operations, performance, and business continuity. Enhanced SLAs provide 50% faster response times during critical phases like go-live.

Portfolio elements across BAIP Technology Foundation (BTP) modules

The services cover platform foundations (BTP administration, security, connectivity), SAP Integration Suite (from foundation to PI/PO migration to custom integrations and governance), application development (SAP Build, ABAP Cloud, Clean Core, DevOps), artificial intelligence (AI Core, Joule, Joule Studio, AI data layer, AI strategy), and automation (process automation, cognitive automation).

For customers with a specific focus on AI, there is a dedicated recommended service plan that covers AI data layer strategy, AI business scenario design, Joule foundations, Joule Studio, and AI Core enablement. And for organizations looking at the broader agentic AI journey, a cross-line-of-business service plan addresses everything from AI orientation and use case navigation to AI trust and compliance, change management, and AI CoE foundation.

Fast Path to Agentic AI

The change management point deserves also some emphasis. When you start introducing AI agents to your workforce and AI agents become an integral part of people's work profiles, that is a significant organizational change. The success plan portfolio includes dedicated organizational change management services delivered by SAP consulting experts. This is not technical change management. It covers the people, process, and governance dimensions that determine whether AI adoption actually sticks.

Customers on the Max Success Plan benefit from services across the full BTP solution lifecycle from Discover through Run covering platform foundation, enterprise integration, application extension, process automation, and artificial intelligence. These services, such as architecture transformation, transformation safeguarding, and business transformation management, are minimum 10 to 15 days in scope and designed for complex, large-scale engagements. Services in this plan are grouped by business scenarios like "Modernize Your Integration Landscape with SAP Integration Suite", "Accelerate Your Business Transformation with a Clean Core", or "Empower Your Business with AI with SAP BTP", which helps customers identify the right entry point.

What does this new Success Plan approach mean for BTP customers?

If you are a BTP customer today, the practical implication is, that you do not need to figure out AI adoption, integration architecture, or platform optimization on your own or in pieces. The success plan model provides structured, expert-led engagement that evolves with your priorities.

The customer examples show the range. One started from zero AI knowledge and ended with a scoped pilot and an enabled team. The other resolved complex architectural decisions and achieved a go-live for 4,200 employees. Both cases share a common thread: a single CSM orchestrating the right experts at the right time, with a service plan that adapts as new questions and priorities emerge. (See the slides below for additional examples). For customers coming from Preferred Success, the transition to the Advanced Success Plan brings more value at the same price point. For organizations with complex landscapes and strategic transformation needs, the Max Success Plan adds the premium services that make a measurable difference.

Next steps

If you want to explore how a Success Plan fits your BTP or AI priorities:

  • Talk to your SAP account team. They can recommend whether the Advanced or Max Success Plan is the right fit, based on your landscape and engagement history.
  • If you already have an engagement (for example, a Preferred Success plan or Premium Engagement contracts), ask about transitioning to the Advanced or Max Success Plan.
  • Reach out to us directly if you are not sure who your SAP contact is - we are happy to help you find the right people.

Questions and Answers from the BAIP Success Plan webinar

Several questions came up during the session. Here are the most relevant ones:

How does the Advanced Success Plan compare to the former Preferred Success? The former Preferred Success had two editions: Standard and Expanded. The Expanded Edition included activation and optimization services and Success Expert engagement, but at a higher price. The Advanced Success Plan now offers those features at the same price as the former Standard Preferred Success. In other words: more value, same investment.

Are there limits on how many services can be consumed? No. As long as services are part of your service plan (created by the CSM and Success Expert), there is no cap. The Japanese customer example with 120+ services in 18 months illustrates the scale that is possible.

Are the activation services different between Advanced and Max? The activation and optimization services are identical. They come primarily from the Advanced tier. Max customers get everything from Advanced plus better SLA and the premium transformation services (cross-solution process improvement, transformation advisory, tailored AI use case adoption). Those premium services are consumed against dedicated premium days.

Can Success Plans be sold through partners? Yes. Success Plans can be sold via the partner channel. In indirect engagements, part of the CSM function is taken over by the partner, who upskills their resources to fulfil that role. There is a clear delineation of responsibilities between SAP and partner, which the account team can provide.

What is covered from the BTP portfolio? Almost all cloudified parts of the BAIP Technology Foundation are covered. This includes Integration Suite, SAP Build, AI Core, Platform Foundation, and related technologies. Third-party products integrated into the BAIP portfolio are not covered.

entry.title: From SAP Analytics Cloud to SAP Engagement Cloud: Creating and Uploading Contact Lists
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC) can be used to analyze customer or contact data and identify a specific target group based on the data available in the underlying model.

In this example, the objective is to use the result of such an analysis to create a contact list in SAP Engagement Cloud, Emarsys edition.

The overall process is:

Data (including Contact Data) is available in Analytical Model in SAC→ Run Analysis in SAC Story → Export → Contact File → SAP Engagement Cloud Import → Contact List → Add Contact List(s) to Segment

This approach can be useful when a target audience is identified through analytical criteria in SAP Analytics Cloud and that selection should subsequently be made available as a contact list in SAP Engagement Cloud.

Prerequisites

For the scenario, the underlying data available to SAP Analytics Cloud should contain the contact attributes required for the subsequent import.

In this example, the most relevant fields are:

  • Email address
  • First name
  • Last name
If the email address is used as the main contact identifier in SAP Engagement Cloud, it must be available for all contacts selected by the SAC Story.

First Name and Last Name enable personalized communication, such as addressing each contact by their first name in an email.

Step 1: Create the Contact Selection in SAP Analytics Cloud

An SAP Analytics Cloud Story based on the relevant contact data should already be available for the analysis and contact selection.

The story can be designed to return the contacts required for a particular marketing use case.

Depending on the underlying model and reporting requirements, the analysis may make use of:

  • Dimensions and key figures
  • Filters
  • Top-N selections
  • Other selection criteria available within the SAC report

The important result for this scenario is that the final report output represents the contacts that should become part of the contact list.

The following example shows an SAC Story in which analytical filters are applied to create the resulting list of contacts.


In this example, filters for Country, Opt-In, Year, Innovation Affinity, Interest in On-Site Events, and State are used to narrow the contact population. Measures such as Number of Activities and Number of Clicks provide additional analytical criteria. The resulting contact selection can then be exported for the subsequent import into SAP Engagement Cloud.

Step 2: Export the SAC Result

Export the resulting contact selection from SAP Analytics Cloud.

The exported dataset serves as the file-based handover between the analytical selection in SAP Analytics Cloud and the contact import into SAP Engagement Cloud.



Export the selected data as a CSV file.
In this example, the export scope is set to Point of View so that the current analytical selection is reflected in the exported result.

Step 3: Prepare the File before importing into SAP Engagement Cloud

Before importing the exported CSV file into SAP Engagement Cloud, a small manual adjustment is required. The file can be opened and edited with a text editor such as Notepad.

The CSV file exported from the SAP Analytics Cloud table contains two header rows. One header row represents the key figures used as columns in the SAC table, while the second header row contains the remaining field names.

For the import into SAP Engagement Cloud, however, we need one consistent header row in which every column has a field name.

Therefore, move the key figure names from the first header row into the corresponding empty positions in the second header row. Afterwards, remove the first header row.

The result is a CSV file with a single, complete header row, followed directly by the contact data.

The following screenshots illustrate the required adjustment.



The names of the two key figures are added to the empty fields in the second row.
Afterwards, the first row is removed, leaving a single, complete header row for the CSV file.



Step 4: Import into SAP Engagement Cloud, Emarsys Edition

The exported contact data can then be used for the contact import in SAP Engagement Cloud, Emarsys edition.

During this step, map the fields from the exported SAC dataset to the corresponding contact fields.

As part of the import process, the imported contacts are assigned to a new contact list.

In SAP Engagement Cloud, navigate to Data Import and select Import Data.



Import the File Manually.



Select the adjusted CSV File.

The exported contact data contains identification and personalization fields, such as email address, First Name and Last Name, as well as additional attributes. The import step maps the required CSV columns to the corresponding contact fields. Only fields relevant to the intended marketing scenario need to be imported.



In the final step, specify a name for the new contact list. The imported contacts will be assigned to this contact list. Depending on whether a contact already exists, the import result distinguishes between newly created and merged contacts.

After the import has completed, the result can be reviewed in the Import History, including the number of newly created and merged contacts and the name of the contact list.



The imported contact list can be used directly in SAP Engagement Cloud, SAP Emarsys edition. Depending on the targeting requirements, it can also serve as the basis for further segmentation.

Combining Multiple Audiences

A combined segment can be useful when contacts from different target groups need to be brought together into one audience.

For example, separate contact lists may have been created from different analytical selections or imports. These lists can first be used as the basis for segments, which can then be brought together in a combined segment. This provides a flexible way to build a broader campaign audience without having to merge the original contact lists.

Conclusion

SAP Analytics Cloud is used to identify and select the relevant target audience based on analytical criteria. The selected contacts are then imported into SAP Engagement Cloud, where the contact list can be used directly or further refined through segmentation.

This provides a simple way to move from analytical audience selection to marketing activation.

entry.title: The Future of Customer Experience Is Connected
entry.content:
For years, customer experience was often viewed as a front-office initiative. 

Marketing owned campaigns. Sales managed opportunities. Service teams handled support. Each function played an important role in shaping the customer journey. 

 

Today, that view is changing. 

 

Customer experience has become a business-wide priority because customers don't interact with organizations in silos. They experience a single brand, whether they're browsing a website, speaking with a salesperson, contacting support, or placing an order. 

The challenge is that many organizations still operate with fragmented customer data and disconnected processes. 

A customer may be known differently across marketing, sales, commerce, and service systems. Valuable insights often remain trapped in departmental applications. And when teams don't share the same view of the customer, delivering a consistent experience becomes significantly more difficult. 

 

That's why the conversation around customer experience is evolving. 

 

It's becoming less about individual interactions and more about connected experiences. 

Organizations are increasingly focused on creating a unified view of the customer, connecting front-office engagement with back-office processes, and enabling employees to make decisions based on complete and accurate information. 

This is where SAP's approach stands out. 

Rather than treating customer experience as a standalone function, SAP continues to connect customer-facing processes with the operational and financial processes that drive the business. By bringing together customer data, commerce, sales, service, and business operations, organizations can create experiences that are not only personalized, but also actionable. 

 

Personalization alone is no longer enough. 

 

Customers expect brands to understand their preferences, anticipate their needs, and deliver consistent experiences across every touchpoint. Meeting those expectations requires more than data. It requires connected data, connected processes, and connected teams. 

The organizations that excel in customer experience won't necessarily be the ones with the most technology. 

They'll be the ones that use technology to create a complete view of their customers and turn that insight into meaningful action. 

As customer expectations continue to evolve, I'd be interested to hear what challenges your organization is seeing. Whether it's customer data, personalization, AI, or cross-functional alignment, let me know. It may become the topic of a future post.

entry.content:
Hi @VasanthaK ,

This is not supported by SAP CPQ-ECC integration.

There is no standard SAP transaction (and no out-of-the-box CPQ integration feature) that takes line items from existing CPQ quotes and appends them to a previously created ECC sales order, nor one that merges multiple CPQ quotes into a single order. This requires custom integration logic.

Note also that CPQ uses transaction for creating a Sales Order (VA01), not editing (VA02).

entry.title: Re: Extending SAP Dynamic Forms with Custom Fields - Disp...
entry.content:
Hi,

Extending Dynamic Forms with custom backend fields does not require you to touch the OData service, create enhancement implementations, or implement BAdIs. The entire extension can be done through two custom event handlers — one for pre-processing (reading backend data into the form) and one for post-processing (extracting form data and writing it back to the backend).

Both handlers subclass /MERP/CL_SDF_EVT_HANDLER_BASE and are configured in Dynamic Forms Agent Settings → Event Processing Tab. SAP ships two standard handlers that serve as excellent reference implementations:

Handler Purpose Class

Pre-processingReads measuring points, characteristics, and classes from the backend into the form/MERP/CL_SDF_EVT_MSRMENT_READ
Post-processingExtracts measurement readings from the form and creates measurement documents via BAPI/MERP/CL_SDF_EVT_CRT_MEAS_DOC

Here's how to build your own pair following the same pattern.

The Four Methods You Override

Both handlers override the same four methods from the base class. The difference is the direction of data flow:

Method Pre-Processing Handler Post-Processing Handler

DEFINE_EVT_ENTITY_MODELDeclares entity types for data you'll read from the backendDeclares entity types for data you'll extract from the form
GET_PARAMETER_LISTExposes configurable parameters (filters, include/exclude flags)Exposes configurable parameters (e.g., notification creation settings)
INITIALIZE_EVT_ENTITY_DATAFetches backend data and populates entity buffersTypically not overridden — post-processing gets data from the form, not the backend
EXECUTECalls GET_FORM_DATA_VIA_MAPPING to push entity data into the formCalls GET_ENTITY_DATA_VIA_MAPPING to pull data out of the form, then persists it

Pre-Processing Handler (Reading Data Into the Form)

Step 1 — Define your entity model. In DEFINE_EVT_ENTITY_MODEL, declare each data entity your handler works with. Each entry maps a logical entity type name to an ABAP structure and indicates cardinality:

METHOD define_evt_entity_model.
  et_entity_model = VALUE #(
    ( evt_entity_type = 'MY_CUSTOM_DATA_TO_FORM'
      ref_struct      = 'ZCUSTOM_FORM_DATA_STR'
      flag_multiple   = abap_true )
  ).
ENDMETHOD.

Step 2 — Declare parameters. In GET_PARAMETER_LIST, expose configuration that administrators can set in the configuration panel without code changes. Each parameter has a name, a DDIC type reference, optional value sets (for dropdowns), and description text. Always call super->get_parameter_list() and append the parent's parameters:

METHOD get_parameter_list.
  et_parameter_info = VALUE #(
    ( param_name        = 'MY_FILTER'
      usage_tabname     = 'ZCUSTOM_FILTER_STR'
      flag_multiple     = abap_true
      param_group       = 'MY_SETTINGS'
      param_grp_label   = 'Custom Data Settings'
      param_description = 'Filter which custom records to fetch' )
  ).

  " Always include parent parameters
  DATA lt_parent TYPE /smfnd/sdf_evt_param_info_tab.
  super->get_parameter_list( IMPORTING et_parameter_info = lt_parent ).
  APPEND LINES OF lt_parent TO et_parameter_info.
ENDMETHOD.

Step 3 — Fetch backend data. In INITIALIZE_EVT_ENTITY_DATA, read parameter values from me->tab_param_value, fetch data from the backend, and populate the entity data buffers in me->tab_evt_entity_data. The standard handler reads measuring points from IMPTT, classes from KLAH/KSSK, characteristics from CABN/CABNT, and characteristic values from AUSP — all joined and filtered based on the configured parameters.

The key pattern:

METHOD initialize_evt_entity_data.
  " 1. Fetch backend data
  SELECT * FROM zcustom_table INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_data)
    WHERE ...

  " 2. Populate entity data buffer
  READ TABLE me->tab_evt_entity_data ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<evt_data>)
    WITH KEY evt_entity_type = 'MY_CUSTOM_DATA_TO_FORM'.
  IF sy-subrc = 0.
    ASSIGN <evt_data>-dref_data->* TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<data_tab>).
    MOVE-CORRESPONDING lt_data TO <data_tab>.
  ENDIF.
ENDMETHOD.

Step 4 — Execute the mapping and form updates. In EXECUTE, call GET_FORM_DATA_VIA_MAPPING to automatically move data from your entity buffers into the form XML using the configured Event Entity Mapping. Optionally manipulate the form directly for anything the standard mapping can't handle:

METHOD execute.
  me->get_form_data_via_mapping(
    EXPORTING
      is_agent_request   = is_agent_request
      iv_df_agent_id     = iv_df_agent_id
      iv_object_type     = iv_object_type
      iv_object_key      = iv_object_key
      it_bo_entity_data  = me->tab_bo_entity_data
      it_evt_entity_data = me->tab_evt_entity_data
    IMPORTING
      ev_error   = DATA(lv_error)
      ev_message = DATA(lv_message)
    CHANGING
      cref_form  = cs_dynamic_form-dref_form ).

  " Optional: direct form manipulation beyond what mapping handles
  " e.g., setting control attributes, injecting metadata/itemsets

  IF gv_data_changed = abap_false.
    ev_no_upd_evt_history = abap_true.
  ENDIF.

  update_preprocessed_form(
    EXPORTING iv_trigger_action = iv_trigger_action
    CHANGING  cs_dynamic_form   = cs_dynamic_form ).
ENDMETHOD.

The standard handler goes further — it manipulates measurement-point controls directly by calling set_node_attribute and set_repeating_grid_node_attr on the form reference to set measurement type, description, limits, UOM, and valuation code itemsets. It even serializes the form XML to inject <fr:metadata> nodes for dropdown lists. You have full flexibility to do the same.

Post-Processing Handler (Writing Data Back to the Backend)

The post-processing handler reverses the flow. The standard handler (/MERP/CL_SDF_EVT_CRT_MEAS_DOC) extracts measurement readings from submitted forms and creates measurement documents via function module MEASUREM_DOCUM_CREATE_SINGLE.

Step 1 — Define your entity model. Same pattern, but the entity types now represent what you'll extract:

METHOD define_evt_entity_model.
  et_entity_model = VALUE #(
    ( evt_entity_type = 'FORM_TO_MY_CUSTOM_DATA'
      ref_struct      = 'ZCUSTOM_FORM_OUTPUT_STR'
      flag_multiple   = abap_true )
  ).
ENDMETHOD.

Step 2 — Declare parameters. The standard post-processing handler exposes three parameters: whether to create a notification for out-of-bounds readings, the notification type, and the notification priority. Same pattern as pre-processing — always call super->get_parameter_list():

METHOD get_parameter_list.
  et_parameter_info = VALUE #(
    param_name = 'TARGET_STATUS' 
    usage_tabname = 'ZCUSTOM_STATUS_STR' 
    usage_fieldname = 'STATUS' 
    param_group = 'POST_PROC_SETTINGS' 
    param_grp_label = 'Post-Processing Settings' 
    param_description = 'Define the target status for records created from form data' 
    field_descriptions = VALUE #( ( fieldname = 'STATUS' value = 'Which status should be set on the created record?' ) ) )
  ).

  DATA lt_parent TYPE /smfnd/sdf_evt_param_info_tab.
  super->get_parameter_list( IMPORTING et_parameter_info = lt_parent ).
  APPEND LINES OF lt_parent TO et_parameter_info.
ENDMETHOD.

Step 3 — Execute: extract form data and persist. This is where the post-processing handler differs most from the pre-processing handler. The EXECUTE method:

  1. Calls super->execute() first (the standard post-processing handler does this)
  2. Calls GET_ENTITY_DATA_VIA_MAPPING to extract form field values into your entity buffers
  3. Optionally reads additional data directly from form controls (for fields not covered by mapping)
  4. Reads parameters, performs business logic, and persists to the backend
  5. Populates ET_PROC_HISTORY with the objects created/changed
METHOD execute.
  ev_no_upd_evt_history = abap_true.

  " 1. Call parent execute
  super->execute(
    EXPORTING iv_df_agent_id    = iv_df_agent_id
              iv_trigger_action = iv_trigger_action
              iv_proc_type      = iv_proc_type
              iv_object_type    = iv_object_type
              iv_object_key     = iv_object_key
              it_bo_entity_data = it_bo_entity_data
              it_evt_entity_data = it_evt_entity_data
              is_agent_request  = is_agent_request
    IMPORTING ev_error   = ev_error
              ev_message = ev_message
    CHANGING  cs_dynamic_form = cs_dynamic_form ).

  " 2. Extract form data into entity buffers via mapping
  me->get_entity_data_via_mapping(
    EXPORTING
      is_agent_request = is_agent_request
      iv_df_agent_id   = iv_df_agent_id
      iv_object_type   = iv_object_type
      iv_object_key    = iv_object_key
      iref_form        = cs_dynamic_form-dref_form
    IMPORTING
      ev_error   = DATA(lv_mapping_error)
      ev_message = DATA(lv_mapping_message)
    CHANGING
      ct_evt_entity_data = me->tab_evt_entity_data ).

  IF lv_mapping_error = abap_true.
    ev_error = abap_true.
    ev_message = lv_mapping_message.
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.

  " 3. Read extracted data from your entity buffer
  READ TABLE me->tab_evt_entity_data ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<evt_data>)
    WITH KEY evt_entity_type = 'FORM_TO_MY_CUSTOM_DATA'.
  CHECK sy-subrc = 0.
  ASSIGN <evt_data>-dref_data->* TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<data_tab>).

  " 4. Loop through extracted records and persist
  LOOP AT <data_tab> ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<record>).
    " Your backend write logic here — BAPIs, direct updates, etc.
    " ...

    " 5. Record what you created/changed in processing history
    APPEND INITIAL LINE TO et_proc_history ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<hist>).
    MOVE-CORRESPONDING cs_dynamic_form TO <hist>.
    <hist>-object_type = 'MY_CUSTOM_OBJ'.
    <hist>-object_key  = lv_created_key.
    <hist>-action      = /syclo/cl_core_constants=>exch_action_insert.

    ev_no_upd_evt_history = abap_false.
  ENDLOOP.
ENDMETHOD.

Key detail from the standard handler: The post-processing handler also reads data directly from form controls when the standard mapping isn't sufficient. The GET_DATA_FROM_MPOINT_CONTROLS method demonstrates this — it iterates over form controls using get_repeating_grid_node_attr (for repeating groups) and get_node_attribute (for single fields), extracting values like reading, valuation code, UOM, and note by their XML attribute names. This is how you handle form controls that have their own internal state beyond what the entity mapping covers.

Configuration (No Code Required After Handler Development)

Once your two handler classes exist, configure them in Dynamic Forms Agent Settings → Event Processing Tab:

  1. Pre-processing event: Set your handler class, Trigger Action = the form lifecycle action (e.g., CREATE), Processing Type = AFTER.
  2. Post-processing event: Set your handler class, Trigger Action = the relevant action (e.g., UPDATE), Processing Type = AFTER.
  3. Event Entity Mapping — For each event, map entity type fields to form XML tags. Each row specifies: entity type, field name, form field tag, form field attribute, and mapping direction. These mappings are what's used in GET_FORM_DATA_VIA_MAPPING and GET_ENTITY_DATA_VIA_MAPPING.
  4. Event Parameters — Set the values for the parameters you declared in GET_PARAMETER_LIST.

Key Documentation

  • Dynamic Forms Agent Settings — Event Processing Tab, Event Entity Mapping, parameters
  • MAIF Installation Guide (PDF) — Documents /MERP/CL_SDF_EVT_HANDLER_BASE and its key methods in the Dynamic Forms Enhancement Points section
  • SAP Dynamic Forms Scenarios — Event Processing lifecycle overview

entry.title: Re: rowcnt cross-database
entry.content:
Finally found an ASE 12.5.4 instance (supports the rowcnt() function) so I can demonstrate a global stored procedure running OP's rowcnt() query ...

Setup:

-- create table in both databases (db1, db2)

create table tab1 (a int, b varchar(100))
go

-- leave the table empty in db1; populate the table in db2

insert tab1 select id,'stuff' from sybsystemprocs..sysobjects
go

-- run a modified copy of OP's query in both databases;
-- results are reformatted for readability

select  db_name() as 'db', object_name(id) as 'table', rowcnt(doampg) as 'rowcnt'
from    sysindexes
where   id = object_id('tab1')
and     indid = 0
go

 db  table rowcnt
 --- ----- ------
 db1 tab1       0
 db2 tab1     477

Wrapping the modified query in a stored procedure wrapper and installing in the sybsystemprocs database:

use sybsystemprocs
go

create procedure sp__rowcnt
@objname varchar(255) ='sysobject'
as

select  db_name() as 'db', object_name(id) as 'table', rowcnt(doampg) as 'rowcnt'
from    sysindexes
where   id = object_id(@objname)
and     indid = 0
go

From the master database we'll run sp__rowcnt against the two tables:

use master
go

exec db1..sp__rowcnt 'tab1'
exec db2..sp__rowcnt 'dbo.tab1'
go

 db  table rowcnt
 --- ----- ------
 db1 tab1       0

 db  table rowcnt
 --- ----- ------
 db2 tab1     477
